title: Lowest Terms Ladder
context: Grade 4, the topic that decides what a tidy fraction looks like. An adult sees cancelling, which is a mechanical move. What is being settled is that both numbers have to travel together, and that reducing is a change of writing and not a change of amount. A child who divides only the upper number has produced a different fraction and will not see it, because the working still looks like cancelling.

writeup.why: Take a fraction down to its tidiest writing by dividing both of its numbers by the same thing, and watch the amount stay exactly where it was.
writeup.look: A fraction at the top of a ladder down the middle of the stage, factor lists under each of its two numbers, and a filled strip down the right.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Lowest Terms Ladder' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the rungs written against the shared factors still waiting in the tray, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each rung is written and the second falling as the tray empties, with the largest factor the two numbers share printed small beside them. Nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The ladder runs down the middle of the working area, 300 wide at 456,202, with rungs 300 by 108 spaced 12 apart, at most five of them, each holding one fraction drawn as an upper number over a level rule 140 by 6 over a lower number. The factor lists open to either side of the top rung, each a row of tiles 64 by 64 at 96,236 and at 804,236, the factors of the upper number on the left and of the lower number on the right, in order and starting from one; a factor standing in both rows is drawn in one shared fill on both, so a common factor is found by looking rather than by being announced. The divider tray is 300 by 76 at 456,150 and holds exactly the shared factors above one, and nothing else, as draggable tiles. Dropping a tile on the fraction divides BOTH numbers by it in one movement and writes the result on the rung below, with a short arrow from each old number to the new one under it. A drag aimed at one of the two numbers alone is handed back with nothing written, both numbers lit together, and the reason printed rather than the answer. When the two rows share nothing above one the tray empties itself and the done light, 180 by 44, comes up beside the last rung. Second ladder opens a parallel ladder at 96,202 from the same starting fraction, with a step count printed under each of the two; when both finish, their two last rungs are joined by a drawn line straight across. The value bar stands down the right of the working area, 76 by 470 at 986,232, a strip of fixed length filled to the amount of the fraction on the current rung and redrawn at every rung, with a faint guide line running left from the first rung's fill level all the way across the ladder. Undo a rung climbs back one step and leaves every rung already written standing where it is. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a rung or a factor is asked for, and beside them a small strip reading factor, common factor and lowest terms, so a step can be named as well as taken. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the parts a fraction counts are deep blue, the parts of that same whole which it leaves are amber, a whole shown entire or a bracket spanning one whole is green, a second writing of an amount already on the stage is rose, the greater of two fractions one of the chapter's rules can settle is vermilion, and a pair neither rule settles is sky blue. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told from the rest by the drawn cut between them and by the label under it before it is ever told by a fill, and every cut, score line, cell edge and guide line is near-black. A fraction is drawn everywhere with its upper number above a level horizontal line and its lower number below, both upright and centred; the line is never slanted and the two numbers are never set side by side. The value bar is never animated as though it were changing. It is redrawn at each rung to exactly the same fill level, which is the one claim a paper working makes and cannot show, and the guide line stays up so that a rung drawn a moment ago can still be measured against the one on the screen now.
writeup.finish: The card shows the ladder the child built, every rung still written, the top and bottom fractions laid side by side and their two value bars drawn against each other.

phases.win: the next rung is written with both numbers smaller, and the single number drag is handed back
phases.does: picks a shared factor and drops it on the fraction, then tries to move one number alone
phases.goal: both numbers are divided, and by the same factor
phases.says: Find something that goes into both numbers. Now divide them both by it.
phases.check: Reduce 6/15 on paper. Tell me which numbers you divided and what you divided each of them by.
phases.feels: one factor, used on both numbers in the same movement, and no other arrangement of the two will go through
phases.hands: On paper write the factors of fourteen in one column and the factors of twenty-one in another, both starting at one, and ring every number that appears in both columns. Only then reduce the fraction, writing the division under each of its two numbers so that both divisions are visible on the page at once.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which numbers are drawn in the same colour in your two lists? Second rung, the phase's: what happens to the other number when you use that one? Third rung: the ladder is cut to a fraction whose two numbers share one factor only, so the tile is chosen before anything has to be found. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: cancelling has been seen as a thing done to a number, and the upper number is the one the eye starts on.
wrong.move: divides the upper number by seven and leaves the lower number standing as it was.
wrong.screen: the drag is handed back with nothing written on the rung below and both numbers lit together. The ladder then draws what that move would have produced on a scratch rung set off to one side, two over twenty-one, with its own value bar beside it; that bar fills to barely a tenth while the bar for fourteen over twenty-one stands at two thirds of the strip, and the guide line runs across both. The child's drag is not repeated for them and nothing is cleared.

wrong.why: both numbers have been divided by something, which is what the rule sounded like, and seven and seven look like a tidy place to end up.
wrong.move: divides the two numbers by different factors, taking two out of the fourteen and three out of the twenty-one.
wrong.screen: the two divisions are written out under their own numbers and both are correct arithmetic, so neither is crossed through. What they build, seven over seven, is drawn on a scratch rung with its value bar, and that bar fills the whole strip because seven parts of something cut into seven is one whole; the bar for fourteen over twenty-one stops two thirds along, and the two are left standing together with the shared factor seven still lit in both lists.

phases.screen: one fraction on the top rung with its two factor lists open
phases.soWhat: Divide the upper number and the lower number by the same common factor, because dividing one of them alone changes the amount rather than the writing.
phases.concept: Dividing both numbers by the same thing

phases.win: the tray empties, the done light comes up and the last rung is ringed
phases.does: checks the two factor lists for anything shared above one and steps again if there is
phases.goal: the fraction is finished when its two numbers share only one
phases.says: Look at both lists. Is there anything left that goes into both?
phases.check: Reduce 42/56 and tell me how you knew you had reached the end.
phases.feels: the numbers being small is not the test at all, and the two lists are
phases.hands: Reduce twenty-four thirty-sixths by dividing both numbers by four, then stop and list the factors of the two numbers you are now holding. Ring anything above one that stands in both lists, and only put the pencil down once there is nothing left to ring.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what are the factors of the two numbers on your last rung? Second rung, the phase's: is there anything above one standing in both lists? Third rung: the lists are cut to the two numbers of the current rung alone and read out together, so the comparison is made before another tile is offered. Nothing already written is taken away.

wrong.why: smaller numbers feel like a finished job, and nothing on a page announces that a fraction still has work left in it.
wrong.move: stops at six over nine because the numbers have got small and the working looks finished.
wrong.screen: both factor lists open under the rung the child stopped on and three comes up drawn the same on each, with the divider tray refilling itself to hold it. The six over nine the child wrote stays on its rung, the next rung is left ruled and empty rather than filled in for them, and the done light stays dark with the tray plainly not empty. Nothing is marked.

wrong.why: a factor of the number being looked at is a real factor, and the word common goes past unnoticed when the number in front of you divides so neatly.
wrong.move: drags a factor that goes into only one of the two numbers, trying two on six over nine because two goes into six.
wrong.screen: the tile springs back without a rung being written, because the tray only ever holds factors standing in both lists. Both lists open with two lit in the six's row and plainly absent from the nine's, and nine is written out against two underneath, going four times with one left over. The tray is then shown holding three, the one factor the two numbers really do share, and nothing is dropped for the child.

phases.screen: a fraction part way down the ladder with the divider tray still holding tiles
phases.soWhat: A fraction is finished only when its two numbers share no factor above one, which is exactly what the two lists are for.

phases.win: both ladders reach the same last rung and the step counts are written beside them
phases.does: takes small steps down one ladder and the largest step down the other
phases.goal: a smaller factor used twice reaches the same rung as the largest used once
phases.says: One of you is taking small steps. Where do you think the two ladders will meet?
phases.check: Which single factor takes 60/84 down in one step, and what does it leave you with?
phases.feels: two ladders of different lengths, standing on exactly the same last rung
phases.hands: Give two children the same fraction, thirty-two over forty-eight, and ask one to halve it as many times as it will go and the other to find the largest factor the two numbers share and use it once. Line the two workings up side by side and count the lines each of them took.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what is the last number standing in both of your lists? Second rung, the phase's: what do the two ladders have written on their bottom rungs? Third rung: the second ladder is cut to one step with its tile already chosen, so the two routes can be compared without either being worked out again. Nothing on either ladder is ever cleared.

wrong.why: two workings of different lengths have meant a mistake in one of them for as long as this child has been checking anything.
wrong.move: decides the longer route must have gone wrong somewhere, because it took three lines where the other took one.
wrong.screen: the two ladders are left standing side by side with every rung on both still written, and the drawn line joins their two last rungs straight across, both reading two over three. The step count under each is printed as a count and not as a mark, three steps and one step, and the value bars beside the two ladders are drawn at the same fill on every rung of both. Neither ladder is ringed and neither is called the better one.

wrong.why: largest is the word that was heard and thirty-two is the largest number in one of the two lists, sitting right there at the end of it.
wrong.move: reaches for thirty-two, the largest factor of the upper number, rather than the largest factor the two numbers share.
wrong.screen: the tile is not in the tray to be dragged, because the tray holds shared factors only, and the reason is drawn rather than stated: forty-eight is written out against thirty-two and goes once with sixteen left over. Both lists are then read down together and the last number standing in both is sixteen, which the tray offers; the child's reach is left drawn as a faint line so the two candidates can be seen at once.

phases.screen: two ladders side by side, both starting from the same fraction
phases.soWhat: The largest common factor finishes in one step, and a smaller one takes more steps and lands in the same place, so a longer route is slower rather than wrong.
phases.concept: The long way and the short way

phases.win: every strip lines up exactly with every other one and the first and last rungs are laid together
phases.does: runs back up and down the ladder watching the filled strip
phases.goal: reducing changes the writing and leaves the value alone
phases.says: The numbers keep getting smaller. Watch the strip beside them.
phases.check: Is 22/33 bigger than 2/3, smaller than it, or the same? Say how you would show me you are right.
phases.feels: the numbers shrink right down the ladder and the strip beside them does not move at all
phases.hands: Draw two identical strips one under the other from the same left edge. Cut the first into thirty-two parts and fill twenty, cut the second into eight and fill five, and lay a ruler across where the colour stops on each. Then write the two fractions underneath and say which of them is the larger.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: where does the colour stop on your top strip? Second rung, the phase's: where does it stop on the one underneath? Third rung: the ladder is cut to its first and last rungs only, laid side by side with their two bars, so the comparison is made on two fractions rather than five. Nothing on the stage is ever marked right or wrong.

wrong.why: smaller numbers have meant a smaller amount in every chapter before this one, and a fraction still looks like a pair of ordinary numbers.
wrong.move: says five eighths must be less than twenty thirty-seconds, because its two numbers are so much smaller.
wrong.screen: the two rungs lift out of the ladder and settle side by side with their value bars drawn against each other and the guide line running through both fills. The strip for twenty over thirty-two carries thirty-two cuts and the strip for five over eight carries eight, and the colour stops in exactly the same place on both. The child's answer stays in the slot and both bars stay drawn.

wrong.why: both numbers moved by the same amount, which is what moving together sounded like, and the numbers did get smaller.
wrong.move: takes four off both numbers instead of dividing both by four, and writes sixteen over twenty-eight.
wrong.screen: the sixteen over twenty-eight the child built is drawn on a scratch rung with a value bar of its own, and it stops visibly short of the guide line that the whole ladder stands on. Beside it the same starting fraction is divided by four in both numbers, landing on five over eight with its bar on the line. Both are left standing, neither is crossed through, and the two moves are printed underneath in the words that tell them apart, taken off and divided by.

phases.screen: the whole ladder with the value bar redrawn beside every rung
phases.soWhat: Reducing changes how a fraction is written and never how much it is worth, which is why the reduced one may be put in place of the one it came from.

writeup.delight: The fourth phase, when a finger runs down and back up the finished ladder. The numbers on the rungs shrink from twenty over thirty-two to five over eight and the value bar is redrawn at every rung as the finger passes it, and it does not move. Not a little, not smoothly, not at all: the fill lands on the guide line each time it is drawn, and the guide line was set by the very first rung. Run the finger back up and the numbers grow again and the bar is redrawn again, still on the line. Then the first rung and the last rung lift out of the ladder and settle side by side with their two bars drawn against each other, twenty over thirty-two beside five over eight, two fills ending in the same place. Nothing else on the stage moves and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase one fraction stands on the top rung with both of its factor lists already open beside it and the shared factor drawn in the same colour on each, and the divider tray below holds one tile. On the second the ladder is part way down, a fraction sits on the third rung and the tray still holds a tile, with the done light drawn and dark. On the third two ladders stand side by side, both carrying the same fraction on their top rungs and both with empty tiles waiting. On the fourth the whole ladder is written out from top to bottom with the value bar drawn beside every rung and a faint guide line running across from the first fill. The running count at the top left holds the rungs written against the shared factors still to use, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the shared factor lit in both lists, or the last tile in the tray, or the second ladder's top rung, or the guide line, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks what these two numbers have in common. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any fraction up to a hundred and forty-four over a hundred and forty-four, with the factor lists, the second ladder and the value bar switched on or off. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on dividing both numbers by one factor, deciding whether a fraction is finished, reaching the same answer by two routes, and showing that the amount did not change.
voiceLines: A fraction at the top of the ladder. Find something that goes into both of its numbers.
Find something that goes into both numbers. Now divide them both by it.
Look at both lists. Is there anything left that goes into both?
One of you is taking small steps. Where do you think the two ladders will meet?
The numbers keep getting smaller. Watch the strip beside them.
Another fraction on the top rung. What do these two numbers have in common?
Free play. Any fraction, the factor lists, a second ladder and the value bar as you like.
Open both factor lists again and look for a number standing in each of them.
Every ladder walked down to its last rung, and the strip beside it never moved at all.

observations.why: Dividing both numbers by one factor takes the same amount and writes it with fewer parts of a bigger size.
observations.soWhat: Reducing changes the writing and not the amount, which is why the reduced fraction may stand in for the one it came from.
observations.observe: The numbers on the last rung were far smaller than the numbers on the first, and the strip beside them filled to exactly the same place.

observations.why: Dividing the upper number alone takes parts away without making the remaining parts any bigger, so a different amount is left.
observations.soWhat: Both numbers travel together or the working has stopped being about the same fraction.
observations.observe: A drag aimed at one of the two numbers was handed back every single time.

observations.why: The largest common factor is every small factor multiplied together, so taking them one at a time arrives in the same place.
observations.soWhat: A longer route is slower and not wrong, which is worth saying to the child who halves and halves again.
observations.observe: Small steps and one large step reached the same last rung, and one ladder had three rungs where the other had two.

observations.why: Both lists always hold one, and one is the factor every pair of numbers shares.
observations.soWhat: A fraction is finished when the only thing its two numbers have in common is one.
observations.observe: The tray emptied itself while there were still factors written in both lists.

description: Divide both numbers of a fraction by the same factor, rung by rung, until only one is left in common.

source_tool.description: A fraction stands at the top rung of a ladder that runs down the middle of the stage, its two numbers stacked over a level rule. Under each number a factor list opens on demand, and the factors the two lists share are drawn in the same colour on both, so a common factor is found by looking rather than by being told. A divider tray offers those shared factors as tiles. Dropping a tile divides BOTH numbers at once and writes the new fraction on the rung below; the two numbers cannot be moved separately, and a drag that tries it is handed back with both numbers lit and the reason printed, because dividing one of them changes the amount rather than the writing. The ladder stops offering tiles when the two lists share nothing but one, and a done light comes up. A second ladder can be opened alongside the first and started from the same fraction, so a child taking small steps and a child taking the largest factor in one go can watch their two ladders arrive on the same rung by different routes. Down the right of the stage runs a value bar, a strip filled to the amount of the fraction, which is redrawn at every rung and does not move, which is the whole point of it.
source_tool.art_direction: A ladder down the stage, a filled strip beside it / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: bars and circles that are cut, paper strips laid from a common left edge, bowls that fill, trays with printed labels, loose parts that slide, and a rail with named gates along it.
A part is never drawn without its whole. Wherever a fraction is shown, the whole it came from stays in the same frame, entire, with the parts nobody took still drawn and still countable.

Every division into parts is made by a drawn cut, a score line or a gap, never by a change of colour alone. The cuts go in before any fill does, so the lower number can be counted whether anything is coloured or not.

Where a fraction says its parts are equal, every part of that whole is drawn the same size and the same shape. Where a stage deliberately shows unequal pieces, it says so in its own label and no fraction name is written against them.

A fraction is always written with its upper number above a level horizontal line and its lower number below it, both upright and centred. The line is never slanted and the two numbers are never set side by side. A mixed number is drawn as an upright whole number beside a stacked fraction.

Two fractions shown to be the same amount are drawn as strips of identical length and width, laid one directly under the other from one common left edge, so that the filled parts ending in the same place is what carries the claim.
Anything the stage asks to be counted is at most twenty things, separated, large enough to count at a glance and never overlapping.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a part, a strip or a token the child is counting, and a content colour is never used for chrome. The parts a fraction counts are deep blue, the parts of that same whole which it leaves are amber, and a whole shown entire or a bracket spanning one whole is green, and those three are the same three colours in every tool and every picture of this chapter. A second writing of an amount already on the stage is rose, so an equivalent fraction is told from the fraction it came from without either being called wrong. The greater of two fractions one of the two rules can settle is vermilion, and a pair that neither rule settles is sky blue, which is how the stage says undecided without saying wrong. All of that holds in greyscale, because a part is told from the rest by the cut line between them and by its label before it is told apart by colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.

voice.onFinish: Every ladder walked down to its last rung, and the strip beside it never moved at all.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any fraction, the factor lists, a second ladder and the value bar as you like.

phase_map.concept: Dividing both numbers by the same thing
The long way and the short way

placement.where: Once one fraction has been reduced on paper with the factors of both numbers listed out by hand. The tool is what holds the value bar still while the numbers shrink, which is the claim a paper working asserts and cannot show.

answer_key.rule: A fraction is in its lowest terms when the only factor its two numbers share is one. To get there, divide the upper number and the lower number by the same common factor, and keep going until nothing but one is left in common. Both numbers must be divided, and by the same thing: dividing one of them alone changes how much the fraction is worth. Using the largest common factor finishes in a single step, and using a smaller one takes more steps and arrives in the same place. Reducing changes the way the fraction is written and never the amount it stands for, which is why the reduced fraction may be put in place of the one it came from.
answer_key.wrong: The two factor lists are opened again with the shared factors lit, and the last rung is rewritten one number at a time so the division can be watched happening to both. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The factors of fourteen are one, two, seven and fourteen, and the factors of twenty-one are one, three, seven and twenty-one.
The only factor above one that they share is seven, so both numbers are divided by seven.
Fourteen divided by seven is two and twenty-one divided by seven is three, giving 2/3.
items.question: Reduce 14/21 by dividing both of its numbers by the same factor.
items.checkpoint: One factor, applied to both numbers at once, is what a reducing step is.
items.misconception: Dividing the upper number by seven and leaving the lower one alone.

steps: Dividing both numbers by four does give 6/9, and that step is correct.
But six and nine both have three as a factor, so something above one is still shared.
Dividing both by three gives 2/3, and two and three share nothing but one, so now it is finished.
items.answer: No. Six and nine still share three, so it goes on to 2/3
items.question: A child reduces 24/36 to 6/9 and stops there. Is the work finished?
items.checkpoint: A fraction is finished only when its two numbers share no factor above one.
items.misconception: Stopping as soon as the numbers look small, without checking the two factor lists.

steps: Halving twice gives 16/24 and then 8/12, and dividing both of those numbers by four gives 2/3.
Sixteen is the largest factor that thirty-two and forty-eight share, and dividing both by it gives 2/3 straight away.
Three steps and one step land on the same rung, so neither route is wrong and one is shorter.
items.question: Reduce 32/48 by halving twice and then dividing by four, and then reduce it again by dividing by sixteen in one step. Do the two agree?
items.checkpoint: The largest common factor is the quickest route, not the only correct one.
items.misconception: Believing that a longer route must have gone wrong somewhere because it took more lines.

steps: Twenty and thirty-two share four, so dividing both by four gives 5/8.
Reducing changes how a fraction is written and not how much it is worth.
So 20/32 and 5/8 are two writings of one amount, and their value bars fill to the same place.
items.question: Is 5/8 less than 20/32, more than it, or the same amount?
items.checkpoint: Reducing tidies the writing and leaves the amount exactly where it was.
items.misconception: Thinking that smaller numbers must mean a smaller amount.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: A child reduces 18/24 to 9/12 and stops. Is that in lowest terms?
items.final_answer: No, because nine and twelve still share three, so it goes on to 3/4

items.question: Reduce 42/56 and say how you knew to stop.
items.final_answer: 3/4, and you stop because three and four share no factor except one

items.question: Reduce 27/45 by dividing by three twice, then check it by dividing by nine in one step.
items.final_answer: 3/5 both ways, since dividing by three twice gives 9/15 and then 3/5

items.question: Which single factor reduces 60/84 in one step, and what does it give?
Is 22/33 bigger than 2/3, smaller than it, or the same?
items.final_answer: The same, because dividing both numbers of 22/33 by eleven gives 2/3

items.question: Reduce 84/108 and say whether the amount changed on the way down.
items.final_answer: 7/9, and the amount did not change at all, only the way it is written

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: opens the factors of both numbers and lights the ones they share
offers the shared factors as tiles that can be dropped on the fraction
divides both numbers by the chosen factor and writes the next rung
opens a parallel ladder from the same starting fraction
draws a strip filled to the amount of the fraction and redraws it at every rung
comes up when the two numbers share no factor but one
climbs back one rung with the working left in place

teaching_notes: List the factors of both numbers by hand before the tool is opened, in two columns, and ring the shared ones. That listing is the part children skip and it is the part that makes the rest possible. Then use the tool for the two things paper will not do. The first is the refusal: let somebody try to divide just the upper number and let the ladder hand it back, and ask what would have happened to the amount if it had gone through. The second is the value bar, which should be on from the first rung to the last. A class that has watched the strip stay exactly still while the numbers halve twice has been given the reason the move is allowed, and will not later think a reduced fraction is a smaller one. Open the second ladder for a fraction with several routes down, such as thirty-two over forty-eight, and put a small-step child beside a largest-factor child. Both are right and one is quicker, and saying that plainly protects the child who halves and halves again. Finish by laying the first and last rungs together, and read them as one amount with two names, because that sentence is the bridge into the next topic.
generation_prompt: Build a reducing tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A fraction sits on the top rung of a ladder drawn down the centre of the working area, its upper number above a level horizontal rule and its lower number below. A factor lists control opens the factors of each number as a row of tiles beside it, with the tiles the two rows share drawn in one shared colour on both rows. A divider tray below offers exactly those shared factors above one as draggable tiles. Dropping a tile on the fraction divides both numbers by it at once and writes the result on the next rung down, with a short arrow from each old number to each new one. A drag aimed at only one of the two numbers is refused, both numbers are lit, and the stage prints that dividing one alone changes the amount. When the two factor rows share nothing above one the tray empties and a done light comes up beside the last rung. A second ladder control opens a parallel ladder from the same starting fraction so two routes can be run side by side, with a step count under each; when both finish, the two final rungs are joined by a drawn line. Down the right of the working area runs a vertical value bar, a strip of fixed length filled to the amount of the current fraction, redrawn at every rung and never changing its fill level, with a faint guide line running across from the first rung's fill. An undo control climbs back one rung leaving the working in place. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Open the two factor lists and look for a number in both. Drop that factor on the fraction to divide both numbers. You cannot move one number without the other. Keep stepping down while anything above one is shared. Watch the strip on the right as you go.
